passages.happening:
The heading reads, “For the choirmaster. A Psalm of the sons of Korah” (verse 1). The psalm starts by remembering mercy. “You showed favor to Your land, O LORD; You restored Jacob from captivity” (verse 1). God forgave his people and turned away his anger (verses 2 to 3).

Yet trouble has come again. So the people ask, “Restore us, O God of our salvation” (verse 4). “Will You be angry with us forever?” (verse 5). “Will You not revive us again, that Your people may rejoice in You?” (verse 6).

Then one voice says, “I will listen to what God the LORD will say; for He will surely speak peace to His people and His saints” (verse 8).

And then comes a picture of everything made right. “Loving devotion and faithfulness have joined together; righteousness and peace have kissed” (verse 10). “Faithfulness sprouts from the earth, and righteousness looks down from heaven” (verse 11). The land will yield its harvest (verse 12). Righteousness will walk ahead of God and prepare his path (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
‘You restored Jacob from captivity’ (verse 1) makes many readers think of the return from exile in Babylon, after Persia took Babylon in 539 BC, as the book page's timeline says. The years after that return were hard. Harvests failed and the people were poor (Haggai 1:6). On this reading the people are saying: God brought us home, so why is it still so hard? Others read the words more widely, as any turning of the people's fortunes. The psalm does not name a year.

For an Israelite, the land and the covenant belonged together. Moses had said that when the people kept faith, the rain and harvests would come. So a first hearer would not see forgiveness (verse 2) and a good harvest (verse 12) as two separate subjects. They were one relationship made whole.

The four words in verse 10 are the great words of God's covenant: loving devotion (hesed), faithfulness, righteousness and peace (shalom). The picture is of four friends meeting and embracing.
passages.later:
Paul says that God showed his righteousness in Jesus, “so as to be just and to justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (Romans 3:26). He also says, “since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 5:1). Christians have often read verse 10 as a picture of the cross, where God's justice and his peace meet.

When Jesus was born, the angels sang of “peace to men on whom His favor rests” (Luke 2:14).
passages.asks:
Have you known God's mercy before, and now find yourself in trouble again? This psalm prays from that place. It remembers past mercy, and asks for it again.

Notice verse 8. Before the beautiful promises, someone chose to listen. When did you last stop and listen for what God might say?
